Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
There is something wrong with me as a person
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, 'being forced to do something' and tactile body-state cues are plausible triggers, but 'burnt smell' introduces a danger cue more typical of fire/explosion trauma and is not supported by the other selected items. It feels disconnected from the stated trauma and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is otherwise self-blaming/defectiveness-focused and tightly linked to triggers, but 'fear of rage' shifts to fear of one's own future violent loss of control. That theme is not supported by the trauma type, the other appraisals, or the maladaptive strategies, making this item difficult to integrate into the same formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time; Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
issues.explanation: The memory items indicate highly severe, here-and-now re-experiencing, which is plausible at this PCL-5 level, but they sit awkwardly with the formulation because Memory has only a weak link to Negative Appraisals and no active links to Triggers or Maladaptive Strategies. Selecting two very strong reliving items plus disorganized narration makes Memory appear more central than the formulation suggests.

vignette: Maya, a 35-year-old South-Eastern Asian physical therapist, married to her college sweetheart for eight years, had become a quiet storm in the clinic. The day her husband turned violent-lifting her in the kitchen and slamming her onto the floor-had been a blur of rage, a sudden cold, damp chill that settled on her forearm, a forceful grip that left her feeling robbed of control. He said nothing, but the memory of his hands tightening around her wrists and the hiss of hot air escaping her skin lingered like a ghostly echo. After that night, the simple sensation of a cool breeze across her skin, the gentle touch of a patient's arm during a routine assessment, or the feeling of being compelled to do something she didn't want, became instant alarms, jolting her into a state of terror that felt as if the past were unfolding anew. When a sudden temperature shift brushed her skin, Maya would retreat inward, obsessively replaying how she had once been a confident, helpful person before the assault. This dwell­ing on the former self became a maladaptive strategy: a mental loop that kept her anchored to a painful past. The same trigger also struck her with sharp self-blame, as she convinced herself the event had been a consequence of her own conduct. The more she blamed herself, the more she felt defective and humiliated, reinforcing her belief that she was somehow broken. These negative appraisals, in turn, propelled her into hypervigilance; she learned to scan every face for potential danger, her eyes flickering as if to catch the slightest sign of threat. Her rumination about what could have been prevented added another layer of dread, and each moment of panic triggered a new sensory cue that she associated with that night. The memory itself-present-feeling, impossible to explain, overwhelming enough to halt her thoughts-fueled the very shame and self-deprecation that kept her in the vicious cycle. In a single, charged paragraph, these interconnections made clear that the tactile and loss-of-autonomy triggers did not merely surface; they activated her maladaptive habits, fed her negative judgments, and perpetuated a loop that now haunted even her professional life. In the clinic, Maya's avoidance of touch had tangible consequences. She now sidestepped the hands-on techniques that were central to her work, substituting verbal guidance whenever a patient asked for a manual assessment. The loss of autonomy that had haunted her domestic life spilled into the workplace: when a colleague asked her to assist in a complex mobilization, Maya's first impulse was to refuse, fearing the handover of control. This refusal cost her a promotion she had worked toward, and it strained her marriage as her husband perceived her reticence as indifference. The hypervigilant stare she gave to each patient's face made it difficult to maintain eye contact, and the constant state of alertness began to drain her energy, leaving her physically exhausted by the end of each shift. The compounding of these maladaptive strategies-past-dwelling, prevention rumination, hypervigilance-kept her locked in a self-reinforcing loop. Each new cold draft or gentle touch sent her spiraling back to the night of the assault, where she found herself unable to articulate the events clearly, the story breaking into fragments as her heart pounded. The overwhelming emotions that seized her whenever the memory resurfaced forced her to stop the conversation abruptly, creating a silent withdrawal that her patients noticed. As a therapist, she could see the pattern: triggers activated negative appraisals; negative appraisals birthed maladaptive behaviors; these behaviors amplified the triggers. The cycle tightened, leaving her feeling trapped between professional obligations and the invisible walls of her trauma. Maya finally decided to seek help after an evening of relentless hypervigilance that left her trembling when a patient whispered a quiet thank you. She realized that the very touch that should have felt healing was now a reminder of cold, forced skin. What frightened her most was the thought that if she could not break the loop, her career and her marriage would continue to crumble under its weight. She hoped therapy would give her a way to untangle the knot of triggers, negative judgments, and maladaptive habits, and that she could once again allow herself to feel safe in a world that no longer whispered threats in every breeze.
